ClearNav: Perception-Aligned Quadrotor Flight Using Differential-Physics

Aditya Azad    Arthur Huang    Guanrui Li ††thanks: *Equal contributors Affiliation: Authors are with Worcester Polytechnic Institute, MA, USA. email: aazad@wpi.edu, gli7@wpi.edu Affiliation: The Author is with Northeastern University, MA, USA. email: huang.arth@northeastern.edu
Abstract

Autonomous quadrotor flight in cluttered environment is an key capability for tasks like inspection and search. Navigation policies trained in simulation and transferred to hardware can fly at high speed in open space, but they can still collide as obstacle clearance shrinks. We attribute most of these collisions to a single mechanism, namely motion in directions the onboard camera does not observe. Heading that is not aligned with the direction of travel and lateral excursion during obstacle avoidance both carry the vehicle toward obstacles outside its field of view. We introduce ClearNav, a navigation policy trained with two reward terms that constrain motion to the observed direction, a forward-looking heading target and a penalty on lateral velocity. A third term penalizes speed near obstacles so that an obstacle entering the field of view remains avoidable. In simulation, across 18 held-out scenarios with 2304 paired flights per policy unseen in training, ClearNav improves success by 6.8 points, cuts the collision rate by 65% relative to the state of the arts, and flies at maximum 5​m/s5$\mathrm{m}\mathrm{/}\mathrm{s}$. For the proximity term alone under matched commanded speeds, the collision reduction still holds at 70%. The effect is significant on static scenes and consistent in direction on moving obstacles, though not significant there at the suite level, showing that safer flight in clutter is possible even on the limited sensors and compute of small drones. We also validate our navigation policy in a real-world cluttered environment, showing that it enables the quadrotor to navigate through the cluttered environment successfully and safely.

I Introduction

Autonomous quadrotor flight in cluttered, confined spaces is a core requirement for search and rescue, and for inspecting forests or collapsed structures. Confined geometry restricts platform size, and thus onboard sensing and compute, so the vehicle must stay safe at small clearances under strict computational budgets.

Classical pipelines decompose navigation into mapping, planning, and control [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8]. Inaccuracies propagate across stages, and the accumulated latency is too high for fast flight in clutter. Hybrid learning-plus-optimization variants recover some latency but still rely on an explicit map [9, 10, 11], as do pure optimization methods [12]. Their fixed-rate replanning leaves less margin as speed grows, and all demand dense sensing with a heavy SWaP burden on small platforms. Imitation learning replaces the pipeline with a direct sensorimotor mapping [13, 14, 15], but the student is bounded by the expert’s performance and degrades out of distribution when the expert uses privileged information [14]. Reinforcement learning removes the expert [16, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22], but its sampled gradients need thousands of parallel environments. Model-based variants trade sample efficiency for a world model whose long-horizon rollouts can fail to generalize [23, 24], and reward shaping reaches the policy only through indirect, high-variance sampled correlations.

Differentiable physics instead differentiates the entire rollout and updates the policy by backpropagation through the simulator [25, 26, 27, 28, 29, 30, 31], an idea that extends to perceptive legged control [32]. Some methods retain an RL actor or critic and are better read as first-order hybrids [33, 34], surveyed in [35]. The analytic gradients generalize to new environments from few simulation samples [27], but differentiating long unrolled rollouts is ill-conditioned and the dynamics Jacobian can become chaotic [36]. The point-mass dynamics sacrifice rotational degrees of freedom, and the privileged shaping signals are unavailable at deployment. As a result, these policies still struggle in environments that need deliberate, multi-step avoidance rather than purely reactive maneuvers: the physics-based rewards that keep training tractable give little incentive for such behavior. Later work shapes the objective with global information available at training time [25, 28], but this oracle is not used to its full potential. In our experiments these approaches fail in cluttered environments, with two recurring causes: misaligned yaw during motion, and overly wide, unsafe trajectories. The point-mass lineage [27] penalizes only the closing-speed component of velocity, leaving tangential motion free. General-purpose GPU frameworks such as DiffAero [37] accelerate training of such policies but are validated on agile-flight benchmarks rather than deliberate avoidance in tight clutter. We introduce a direction-agnostic speed-proximity cost as one term in a navigation objective for tight clutter, paired with heading and strafe-aware penalties.

To address this gap, we introduce ClearNav, a safer differentiable-physics policy for cluttered spaces. ClearNav adds three reward terms to an already-tuned differentiable-rollout objective [25], chosen so that no degree of freedom is sacrificed.

Specifically, the contributions of this work are:

  • •

    Safer navigation in cluttered environments: We penalize high speed near obstacles, misaligned yaw, and excessive strafing. Each penalized behavior is observable at inference time, so the policy keeps the information it needs to act on the objective during deployment.

  • •

    Navigation around large obstacles: Our policy navigates around obstacles across a wide range of sizes, shapes, and counts across simulations and real world experiment including large obstacles.

  • •

    Thorough simulation experiments: We compare against other exisiting approaches on static out-of-distribution scenes, a matched-velocity control, moving obstacles, and a cross-framework setting.

II Methodology

This section describes how the policy is trained. Section II-A states the navigation problem and defines the observation and action. Section II-B introduces the differentiable point-mass dynamics that let us backpropagate through entire rollouts. Section II-C describes the Habitat training scenes and the geodesic guidance field that shapes the objective without entering the policy. Section II-D presents the three-branch recurrent policy architecture. Section II-E details the per-step objective and the three loss terms we add to it. Section II-E7 describes the two-stage training procedure that carries the weights from an empty arena into cluttered scenes.

II-A Problem formulation

A quadrotor flies autonomously from a randomly sampled start pose to a goal position 𝒑g∈ℝ3\bm{p}_{g}\in\mathbb{R}^{3} through an unknown, cluttered environment, using only a forward-facing depth camera and proprioception. We use three frames (Fig. 2): an ENU world frame 𝒲\mathcal{W}, a start frame 𝒮\mathcal{S} fixed at the reset pose, and a body frame ℬ\mathcal{B} at the center of mass, with rotations Rw​s,Rw​b∈S​O​(3)R_{ws},R_{wb}\in SO(3). At each step tt the policy receives the observation

𝒐t=(𝒔t,𝒈t,Dt),\bm{o}_{t}\;=\;\bigl(\,\bm{s}_{t},\;\bm{g}_{t},\;D_{t}\,\bigr), (1)

where the proprioceptive state 𝒔t∈ℝ7\bm{s}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{7} stacks the attitude quaternion of ℬ\mathcal{B} relative to 𝒮\mathcal{S} and the velocity expressed in 𝒮\mathcal{S}, both perturbed by Gaussian noise resampled every step. The goal encoding 𝒈t∈ℝ4\bm{g}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{4} is a clamped proportional velocity command 𝒗tcmd=min⁡(Kp​‖𝒑g−𝒑t‖,v⋆)​(𝒑g−𝒑t)^\bm{v}^{\mathrm{cmd}}_{t}=\min(K_{p}\|\bm{p}_{g}-\bm{p}_{t}\|,\,v^{\star})\,\widehat{(\bm{p}_{g}-\bm{p}_{t})}, where KpK_{p} is a proportional gain and v⋆v^{\star} is the command speed cap, together with an inverse range [max⁡(‖𝒑g−𝒑t‖,dmin)]−1[\max(\|\bm{p}_{g}-\bm{p}_{t}\|,\,d_{\min})]^{-1}, with dmin=0.5d_{\min}=0.5 m, and the hat (⋅)^\widehat{(\,\cdot\,)} denotes the normalized unit vector of a vector. The command points straight at the goal and carries no obstacle information, so all avoidance must come from the depth image Dt∈ℝ1×H×WD_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times H\times W} of height HH and width WW, whose invalid returns are set to the far plane and treated as free space.

The action is a mass-normalized collective thrust vector 𝒇t\bm{f}_{t} in 𝒮\mathcal{S} plus an absolute yaw setpoint ψt\psi_{t},

𝒂t=(𝒇t,ψt)∈ℝ3×(−π,π].\bm{a}_{t}=\bigl(\bm{f}_{t},\;\psi_{t}\bigr)\in\mathbb{R}^{3}\times(-\pi,\pi]. (2)

We denote our navigation policy as πθ\pi_{\theta}, parameterized by θ\theta. The navigation policy will take observation 𝒐t\bm{o}_{t} and the policy’s recurrent state 𝒉t\bm{h}_{t} as input and output control action 𝒂t\bm{a}_{t}, so 𝒂t=πθ​(𝒐t,𝒉t)\bm{a}_{t}=\pi_{\theta}(\bm{o}_{t},\bm{h}_{t}). Since the simulator is differentiable end to end, we optimize θ\theta directly rather than via policy gradients:

minθ⁡𝔼⁡[1H​∑t=0H−1γt​ℒ​(𝒙t,𝒂t)],\min_{\theta}\;\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\,\tfrac{1}{H}\!\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\gamma^{t}\,\mathcal{L}\bigl(\bm{x}_{t},\bm{a}_{t}\bigr)\Bigr], (3)

where 𝒙t\bm{x}_{t} is the full simulator state, HH the rollout horizon, and the expectation is over initial conditions, scenes, and the injected noise. The gradient ∂ℒ/∂θ\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial\theta is obtained by backpropagation through the unrolled dynamics (Sec. II-E7).

II-B Differentiable dynamics

The vehicle is modeled as a point mass with an attitude reconstructed from the commanded thrust and yaw [25, 27], an abstraction that can struggle where significant yaw motion is required. Translational dynamics are integrated with velocity Verlet at step Δ​t\Delta t under net acceleration 𝒂tnet=Rw​s​𝒇t+𝒈\bm{a}^{\mathrm{net}}_{t}=R_{ws}\bm{f}_{t}+\bm{g},

𝒑t+1\displaystyle\bm{p}_{t+1} =𝒑t+𝒗t​Δ​t+12​𝒂tnet​Δ​t2,\displaystyle=\bm{p}_{t}+\bm{v}_{t}\Delta t+\tfrac{1}{2}\bm{a}^{\mathrm{net}}_{t}\Delta t^{2}, (4)
𝒗t+1\displaystyle\bm{v}_{t+1} =𝒗t+12​(𝒂tnet+𝒂t+1net)​Δ​t.\displaystyle=\bm{v}_{t}+\tfrac{1}{2}\bigl(\bm{a}^{\mathrm{net}}_{t}+\bm{a}^{\mathrm{net}}_{t+1}\bigr)\Delta t. (5)

Gravity 𝒈\bm{g} is resampled per episode from 𝒩⁡(−9.81​𝒆3,σg2)\mathcal{N}(-9.81\,\bm{e}_{3},\sigma_{g}^{2}) on the vertical axis, where 𝒆3\bm{e}_{3} is the world vertical unit vector and σg\sigma_{g} is the gravity noise standard deviation, which absorbs unmodeled mass and thrust-coefficient error.

Attitude is not integrated. Given the filtered thrust command 𝒇\bm{f} and yaw setpoint ψ\psi, the body frame is reconstructed in closed form from its axes 𝒙b,𝒚b,𝒛b\bm{x}_{b},\bm{y}_{b},\bm{z}_{b} so that 𝒛b\bm{z}_{b} is along the thrust and 𝒙b\bm{x}_{b} is as close as possible to the commanded heading 𝒉=Rw​s​Rz​(ψ)​𝒆1\bm{h}=R_{ws}R_{z}(\psi)\bm{e}_{1}, where Rz​(ψ)R_{z}(\psi) rotates about the vertical axis by ψ\psi and 𝒆1\bm{e}_{1} is the start-frame forward axis, with 𝒚b\bm{y}_{b} completing the right-handed orthonormal triad,

𝒛b=𝒇^,𝒚b=𝒛b×𝒉^,𝒙b=𝒚b×𝒛b^,\bm{z}_{b}=\widehat{\bm{f}},\quad\bm{y}_{b}=\widehat{\bm{z}_{b}\times\bm{h}},\quad\bm{x}_{b}=\widehat{\bm{y}_{b}\times\bm{z}_{b}}, (6)

with degenerate cases handled by fixed fallbacks. Body rate 𝝎\bm{\omega}, recovered by finite-differencing consecutive rotations, is differentiable and penalized directly.

Unrolling (5) for hundreds of steps produces the same ill-conditioning that afflicts long BPTT chains. To solve this, gradients flowing back through the BPTT rollout are shrunk by e−λd​Te^{-\lambda_{d}T} over a horizon TT, bounding the total gain.

II-C Environment and geodesic guidance

Training scenes are built on Habitat-sim [38]. The nearest-obstacle query is exact: the closest surface point 𝒄t\bm{c}_{t} gives a signed clearance

dt=‖𝒄t−𝒑t‖−r,d_{t}\;=\;\|\bm{c}_{t}-\bm{p}_{t}\|-r, (7)

where rr is the vehicle’s collision radius. An episode terminates in collision when dt<0d_{t}<0 or on leaving the stage, and in success when ‖𝒑g−𝒑t‖<rsucc\|\bm{p}_{g}-\bm{p}_{t}\|<r_{\mathrm{succ}}.

𝒖^​(𝒑)=−∇Ψ​(𝒑)^\widehat{\bm{u}}(\bm{p})\;=\;-\widehat{\nabla\Psi(\bm{p})} (8)

where Ψ\Psi is the scalar time-of-arrival potential and 𝒖^\widehat{\bm{u}} is its unit descent direction. This field is privileged, only shaping the objective and never an input to πθ\pi_{\theta}.

II-D Policy architecture

πθ\pi_{\theta} is a three-branch encoder followed by a single recurrent cell and a linear head (Fig. 3). The depth branch inverts the range map, D~=1/(D+ϵ)\tilde{D}=1/(D+\epsilon), then max-pools it to a coarse H′×W′H^{\prime}\times W^{\prime} grid. Max-pooling inverse depth preserves the closest obstacle in each cell. Three stride-1 convolutions with 32/64/12832/64/128 channels and leaky-ReLU, a linear projection to nfn_{f}, and layer normalization follow. The state and goal branches are each a layer-normalized MLP to width nfn_{f}.

The three feature vectors are summed, layer-normalized, passed through a GRU cell of width nfn_{f}, and mapped by one linear layer to an unbounded thrust vector and a yaw angle squashed by a sigmoid into (−π,π](-\pi,\pi]. The whole network is ≈2.2\approx\!2.2M parameters, which can run on many low power single board computers.

II-E Objective

The per-step cost is a weighted sum of nine terms. Writing 𝒗¯\bar{\bm{v}} for the uniform moving average of velocity over a window TavgT_{\mathrm{avg}}, 𝒗¯e\bar{\bm{v}}^{\,e} for its exponentially weighted counterpart, 𝒗b=Rw​b⊤​𝒗\bm{v}_{b}=R_{wb}^{\!\top}\bm{v} for the velocity expressed in ℬ\mathcal{B}, and 𝒄^t\widehat{\bm{c}}_{t} for the unit vector toward the nearest obstacle,

ℒ=\displaystyle\mathcal{L}\;= λv​ℒv+λv¯​ℒv¯+λc​ℒc+∑k∈{a,j,ω}λk​ℒk\displaystyle\lambda_{v}\mathcal{L}_{v}+\lambda_{\bar{v}}\mathcal{L}_{\bar{v}}+\lambda_{c}\mathcal{L}_{c}+\!\!\!\sum_{k\in\{a,j,\omega\}}\!\!\!\lambda_{k}\mathcal{L}_{k} (9)
+λoa​ℒoa+λslip​ℒslip+λψ​ℒψ\displaystyle}{\displaystyle+\lambda_{\mathrm{oa}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{oa}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{slip}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{slip}}+\lambda_{\psi}\mathcal{L}_{\psi}

and the reward reported in the logs is r=−ℒr=-\mathcal{L}.

II-E1 Progress

The vehicle is asked to track the routed direction at the commanded speed, penalized with a Huber loss on the magnitude of the tracking error, plus a one-sided quadratic that discourages exceeding the commanded speed:

ℒv\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{v} =huber⁡(‖v⋆​𝒖^−𝒗¯‖),\displaystyle=\mathrm{huber}\bigl(\,\|v^{\star}\widehat{\bm{u}}-\bar{\bm{v}}\|\,\bigr), (10)
ℒv¯\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\bar{v}} =(‖𝒗‖−v⋆)+2.\displaystyle=\bigl(\|\bm{v}\|-v^{\star}\bigr)_{+}^{2}. (11)

Using the windowed average 𝒗¯\bar{\bm{v}} rather than the instantaneous velocity in (10) is what allows a lateral excursion around an obstacle without being immediately penalized for it.

II-E2 Collision

The safety term combines a closing-speed penalty with a soft interior barrier,

ℒc=(𝒗⋅𝒄^)+​(df−d)+2⏟closing speed+β1​log⁡(1+eβ2​d)⏟barrier,\mathcal{L}_{c}=\underbrace{\bigl(\bm{v}\!\cdot\!\widehat{\bm{c}}\bigr)_{+}\bigl(d_{f}-d\bigr)_{+}^{2}}_{\text{closing speed}}\;+\;\underbrace{\beta_{1}\log\!\bigl(1+e^{\beta_{2}d}\bigr)}_{\text{barrier}}, (12)

Here dd is the clearance dtd_{t} from (7), and β2<0\beta_{2}<0 so the barrier is negligible for d≫0d\gg 0 and grows linearly once the surface is penetrated. The closing-speed factor penalizes radial approach within a shell of thickness dfd_{f}.

II-E3 Smoothness

ℒa=‖𝒂‖2\mathcal{L}_{a}=\|\bm{a}\|^{2}, ℒj=‖𝒋‖2\mathcal{L}_{j}=\|\bm{j}\|^{2} and ℒω=‖𝝎‖2\mathcal{L}_{\omega}=\|\bm{\omega}\|^{2} penalize acceleration, jerk, and body rate, where here 𝒂\bm{a} is the translational acceleration and 𝒋\bm{j} the jerk, making trajectories flyable.

II-E4 Heading

The heading reference interpolates along the great circle from the goal direction to the smoothed velocity direction, since early in an episode there is no motion to look along,
